title: Forced changes in Atlantic overturning are distinctly fingerprinted by South Atlantic western boundary transports
abstract: Abstract As a major ocean circulation system, the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) may approach a critical transition under anthropogenic forcing, yet how large-scale AMOC changes imprint on regional circulation pathways remains incompletely understood. While persistent changes in overturning are expected to be meridionally coherent, their horizontal expression may be highly non-uniform. Here, we use 22,000-year-long transient deglacial climate simulations to examine how latitudinally coherent AMOC variations are redistributed across the upper Atlantic circulation. By separating externally forced, long-term AMOC changes from internally generated, short-term variability, we show that the former are disproportionately reflected along the full meridional extent of the South Atlantic western boundary current system. In contrast, North Atlantic counterparts relate primarily to higher-frequency, unforced AMOC variability. Our findings highlight South Atlantic western boundary transports as outstanding fingerprints of past externally forced AMOC changes, thereby outlining their particular sensitivity to a predicted, anthropogenically forced weakening of the AMOC.
problem: How large-scale, coherent changes in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) imprint non-uniformly on regional circulation pathways is incompletely understood, challenging efforts to identify clear fingerprints of externally forced climate change.
method: We use 22,000-year-long transient deglacial climate simulations to separate externally forced, long-term AMOC changes from internally generated, short-term variability, thereby analyzing their distinct imprints on the South Atlantic western boundary current system to identify robust fingerprints of forced AMOC change.
task: The task is to use 22,000-year-long climate simulations to examine how externally forced, long-term changes in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) are distinctly reflected in the transports of the South Atlantic western boundary current system, identifying them as robust fingerprints.

innovation: Using 22,000-year-long climate simulations, this paper demonstrates that externally forced, long-term changes in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) are disproportionately reflected by the South Atlantic western boundary transports, identifying them as outstanding fingerprints for monitoring and predicting AMOC weakening.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: By separating externally forced, long-term AMOC changes from internally generated, short-term variability, we show that the former are disproportionately reflected along the full meridional extent of the South Atlantic western boundary current system. In contrast, North Atlantic counterparts relate primarily to higher-frequency, unforced AMOC variability. Our findings highlight South Atlantic western boundary transports as outstanding fingerprints of past externally forced AMOC changes, thereby outlining their particular sensitivity to a predicted, anthropogenically forced weakening of the AMOC.

By separating externally forced, long-term AMOC changes from internally generated, short-term variability, we show that the former are disproportionately reflected along the full meridional extent of the South Atlantic western boundary current system. In contrast, North Atlantic counterparts relate primarily to higher-frequency, unforced AMOC variability. Our findings highlight South Atlantic western boundary transports as outstanding fingerprints of past externally forced AMOC changes, thereby outlining their particular sensitivity to a predicted, anthropogenically forced weakening of the AMOC.

The primary, upper AMOC cell (herein referred to as simply “AMOC”) ventilates the upper ~2 km of the ocean, emanating from the northern North Atlantic (NA) with the for-mation of North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW), which is transported southward along the AMOC lower limb. A compensating return flow occurs at shallower depths, as interocean thermocline and intermediate waters are carried northward along the AMOC upper limb²³.

Meanwhile, the extent to which the AMOC influences the South Atlantic (SA) in the long term is clearly illustrated by mean-state deviations of expected volume and heat transports. The SA is the only ocean basin that counterintuitively exports heat toward the Equator, so as to balance NA heat piracy³⁴. Its western boundary (WB) Brazil Current (BC) is also strikingly weak among global counterparts, as most South Atlantic subtropical gyre (SASG) waters escape northward through the North Brazil Undercurrent (NBUC), analogously balancing NADW export³⁵.
